segments.t: At his quiet Parisian apartment, an exhausted Mathias Barneville receives an unexpected visit from his devoted assistant Noemie. Noticing his overwhelming stress from agency battles, Noemie steps in to comfort him and ease his physical tension with a soothing massage. Listen to the scene in French first. Don't worry about catching every word.
C'est une super nouvelle pour Adjani!
Je ne me sens pas bien.
Je ne suis pas fan des massages.
Tu avais juste besoin de repos.
Now let's break down the scene step by step. Listen to each line, followed by its meaning and a short explanation.
'Is everything going well, Mathias?' Swapping 'everything' into the casual 'it goes well?' pattern gives a caring check-in you can say anywhere.
'Can I come in for a moment?' Notice French needs no 'for' before 'an instant', keeping the doorway question light and natural.
'Of course, do come in.' Adding a short softener that usually means 'therefore' right after a command warms it into 'do come on in!' in French.
'I would have tidied up if I had known.' Just as in English, French pairs 'would have tidied' with 'if I had known' to express polite hindsight.
'I have nothing to offer you.' Linking 'nothing' to 'offer' takes single-letter 'to', with shortened casual 'you' attached right onto 'offer' in French.
C'est une super nouvelle pour Adjani!
'That is great news for Adjani!' Casual 'super' never changes its spelling or sound before any word in French, making it effortless to use.
'Yes, everything is well sorted out.' Slipping 'well' ahead of 'settled' reassures Noemie that every loose end is tied up in French.
Je ne me sens pas bien.
'I do not feel well.' While 'smell' in scene one used this same action alone, adding 'myself' before it shifts the meaning to 'feel' physically in French.
'Sit down in this armchair.' Notice you sit 'on' an armchair in French rather than 'in' it as English speakers usually say.
Je ne suis pas fan des massages.
'I am not a fan of massages.' Taken straight from English, 'fan' links to 'the massages' using 'of the' in French.
'Let me eliminate all this tension.' Both 'eliminate' and 'tension' are transparent cognates, introduced by 'let-me' with no extra word between them.
'Breathe calmly and relax.' Adding '-ment' onto 'calm' works just like adding '-ly' in English, joined by 'and' to casual 'relax-yourself'.
'Oh yes, that is truly excellent.' Notice the cognate 'excellent' carries nasal vowels in French and leaves its final 't' silent.
Tu avais juste besoin de repos.
'You just needed some rest.' After 'had need of', French uses bare 'rest' without 'some', related to English 'repose'. Now let's listen to the whole exchange once more from beginning to end.
C'est une super nouvelle pour Adjani!
Je ne me sens pas bien.
Je ne suis pas fan des massages.
Tu avais juste besoin de repos.
As the tension melts away under Noemie's touch, the bond between the two partners deepens outside the walls of ASK. See you next time!
